clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant spastic paraplegia caused by REEP1 variants, a common cause of pure hereditary spastic paraplegia after SPG4
REEP1 shapes the tubular endoplasmic reticulum and interacts with spastin and atlastin, linking SPG31 to the same axonal membrane-modelling network
Typically presents as a pure phenotype with slowly progressive lower-limb spasticity, brisk reflexes and extensor plantar responses
Age at onset is often bimodal, with peaks in the first two decades and again in later adult life
Some individuals show distal wasting or a mild peripheral neuropathy, giving a complicated flavour in a minority
Penetrance is high but expression varies within families, so mildly affected relatives may be overlooked
Management is symptomatic: physiotherapy, spasticity control, orthoses and falls prevention
reference.pathophysiology: SPG31 is caused by heterozygous variants in REEP1, which encodes a receptor expression-enhancing protein enriched in the endoplasmic reticulum of neurons. REEP1 helps generate and stabilise the curved tubular endoplasmic reticulum and cooperates with spastin (SPG4) and atlastin (SPG3A) in modelling this network along the axon, and it also influences mitochondrial interactions and lipid handling. Disruption of endoplasmic reticulum architecture and axonal organelle distribution impairs maintenance of the longest corticospinal axons, producing a length-dependent distal axonopathy that presents clinically as slowly progressive spastic paraparesis.
additionalDifferentials: SPG4 (spastin) and SPG3A (atlastin) hereditary spastic paraplegia
Other pure dominant hereditary spastic paraplegias
additionalInvestigations: REEP1 sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis within a hereditary spastic paraplegia panel
MRI of brain and spine to exclude acquired myelopathy
Nerve conduction studies where distal wasting suggests a complicated form
Assessment of first-degree relatives given variable expression
Very-long-chain fatty acids and B12 to exclude metabolic mimics
Urodynamic assessment if bladder symptoms develop
redFlags: A sensory level or sphincter emergency suggesting acquired cord compression
Unusually rapid progression atypical for hereditary spastic paraplegia
Marked bulbar or widespread lower motor neurone signs prompting reassessment
Prominent cognitive or cerebellar features suggesting an alternative diagnosis
reference.prognosis: SPG31 usually follows a slowly progressive course with prolonged preservation of walking, and later-onset cases may remain relatively mild throughout life.
pitfalls: Stopping genetic testing after a negative SPG4 result, missing the second most common pure HSP gene
Missing deletion or duplication variants if only sequencing is performed
Overlooking mildly affected relatives when assessing inheritance
Attributing a bimodal-onset family to two separate disorders
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: No disease-modifying therapy exists; manage lower-limb spasticity with oral antispasticity agents such as baclofen or tizanidine and focal botulinum toxin for focal hypertonia
Physiotherapy, stretching and ankle-foot orthoses with walking aids to preserve gait and prevent contractures
Treat neurogenic bladder symptoms with antimuscarinic agents alongside urological review
Podiatry and orthotic support where distal wasting or peripheral neuropathy complicate the picture
Consider intrathecal baclofen for spasticity refractory to oral and focal treatment
Genetic counselling and cascade REEP1 testing for autosomal dominant inheritance, examining mildly affected relatives given variable expression
Escalate to multidisciplinary rehabilitation as mobility declines
